metadata.title: Fostering Self-efficacy: Understanding South African Grade 9 Students’ Confidence in their Mathematics Abilities
metadata.venue: African Journal of Research in Mathematics, Science and Technology Education

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 9 mathematics contextual and achievement data for South Africa, with a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design (schools stratified by province and school type; classes sampled within schools). The authors report that all data were weighted to the full population of Grade 9 students in South Africa (N = 876,525) using the Department of Basic Education’s master list of schools to ensure representativeness. They also state that the analysis was performed using the IEA International Database Analyser (v5), which accounts for the complex sampling design and utilises plausible values methodology. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight usage cannot be confirmed.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that mathematics achievement scores were based on five plausible values and that the IEA International Database Analyser (v5) was used, which implies proper plausible-value estimation. However, it does not describe how missing questionnaire responses or missingness in constructed indices were handled (e.g., complete-case vs imputation). Given the use of complex survey procedures and PVs, the absence of an explicit missing-data strategy is a reporting gap that limits assessment of potential bias.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 South Africa Grade 9 mathematics assessment data with the full nationally representative sample of participating Grade 9 students (20,829 students from 524 schools). The paper does not report additional analytic exclusions beyond the standard TIMSS sampling and the requirement that students completed the mathematics contextual questionnaire items used to construct the self-efficacy and contextual scales.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple regression (adjusted R2 not reported for this model); coefficients reported: Gender β = -0.20 (p < 0.01), Age β = 0.01 (p = 0.9), SES β = 0.01 (p = 0.1), Instructional clarity β = 0.23 (p < 0.01), Parents set homework time β = 0.06 (p not significant), Parents check homework β = 0.32 (p < 0.01), Maths achievement β = 0.01 (p < 0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 9 Mathematics data for South Africa, the study leveraged Gender (girl), Age, Home socioeconomic status, Instructional clarity, and Parents check homework to model self-efficacy in mathematics, finding that self-efficacy was significantly higher for students with greater instructional clarity and for those whose parents checked homework, while females reported lower self-efficacy even after accounting for achievement and contextual factors. This indicates that classroom instructional practices and active parental homework monitoring are actionable levers for strengthening students’ mathematics confidence, though the cross-sectional design limits causal direction.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple regression: adjusted R2 = 0.15 (p < 0.00); self-efficacy coefficient reported as β = 0.01 per standard deviation increase in mathematics achievement (p < 0.01). Bivariate associations (Table 2) reported as significant at p < 0.01 for all variables.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 9 Mathematics data for South Africa, the study leveraged self-efficacy alongside Gender (girl), Home socioeconomic status, Instructional clarity, and Parents check homework to explain mathematics achievement, finding that self-efficacy remained significantly and positively linked to mathematics achievement after controlling for background characteristics. This indicates that interventions aimed at improving students’ mathematics self-beliefs may support achievement gains in resource-constrained contexts, though the study’s cross-sectional regression framework cannot establish whether self-efficacy causes achievement.

data.outcome_summary: This open-access study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 9 mathematics data for South Africa (20,829 students from 524 schools) to examine how mathematics self-efficacy relates to mathematics achievement and which contextual factors are associated with self-efficacy. The authors use the IEA International Database Analyser (v5) to account for the complex sampling design and plausible values methodology; mathematics achievement is reported on a common scale centered at 500 with a standard deviation of 100 and is based on five plausible values. In multiple regression, the model explains 15% of the variation in mathematics achievement (adjusted R2 = 0.15), and self-efficacy is reported as significantly and positively associated with achievement even after controlling for age, SES, instructional clarity, and home experiences. For self-efficacy, instructional clarity and parents checking homework show positive associations, while females report lower self-efficacy after controls. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (directionality cannot be established) and the lack of an explicit missing-data handling description.
